title: Game Engine Lineage Atlas
description: Expanded game engine families, forks, source ports, company ecosystems, notable games and esports-tagged titles.

curriculumPresets.title: Full atlas
curriculumPresets.description: Explore every engine family, game, source port, mod and relationship in the dataset.

curriculumPresets.title: L3 Unit 9 A: compare esports games
curriculumPresets.description: Compare games from different genres. Explain how engine constraints, mechanics, rules, feedback, pacing and replayability affect competitive viability and audiences.

curriculumPresets.title: L3 Unit 9 B: research current concepts
curriculumPresets.description: Use current titles and engine families as case studies, then record which ideas are being adopted, adapted or rejected after research and feedback.

curriculumPresets.title: L3 Unit 9 C: technical requirements
curriculumPresets.description: Focus on engine families and tools when justifying platform, functionality, production constraints and practical requirements in a game design document.

curriculumPresets.title: L2 Unit 6: simplified esports view
curriculumPresets.description: A reduced view for identifying design principles and linking engine or platform choices to mechanics, genre and esports suitability.

nodes.name: Game Engine Lineage Atlas
nodes.note: A teaching map of engine inheritance, licensing, forks, source ports, company ecosystems and influential releases. Treat it as a lineage model, not a complete legal/code audit. Updated to include stronger notable-game coverage, company ecosystems and esports tags.
nodes.hook: Use this to separate five ideas students often blur: engine, game, mod, source port, commercial fork and spiritual successor.

nodes.name: id Software FPS lineage
nodes.note: The core FPS technology lineage running from Wolfenstein/Doom through Quake and the modern id Tech engines.
nodes.hook: Strong teaching case for iterative engine development: renderer, networking, tools, scripting and licensing evolve separately.

nodes.name: Wolfenstein 3D engine
nodes.note: Ray-casting era before Doom's sector-based maps. Useful pre-history for explaining why Doom felt technically different.
nodes.hook: Compare corridor ray-casting with sector-based level design and true polygonal 3D.

nodes.name: Doom engine / id Tech 1
nodes.note: Sector-based 2.5D engine. Its source release helped create a huge source-port ecosystem.
nodes.hook: Excellent for lessons on how technical constraints shape level design: sectors, linedefs, sprites and fake verticality.

nodes.name: Heretic
nodes.note: Fantasy shooter using Doom-family technology; inventory and vertical look ideas make it useful for design comparison.
nodes.hook: Ask students how a small mechanical addition changes level pacing and player choice.

nodes.name: Hexen
nodes.note: Doom-family engine with hub-based progression and classes.
nodes.hook: Good example of genre hybridisation inside an existing engine.

nodes.name: Strife
nodes.note: Blends Doom-like action with dialogue and questing.
nodes.hook: Useful example for showing that engine lineage does not force one genre.

nodes.name: Boom compatibility
nodes.note: A key Doom source-port compatibility target that extended mapping features.
nodes.hook: Use as a standards discussion: community compatibility levels can become design targets.

nodes.name: MBF
nodes.note: Marine's Best Friend extended Boom with extra behaviours and code features.
nodes.hook: Good for showing small source changes becoming visible gameplay affordances.

nodes.name: Chocolate Doom
nodes.note: Accuracy-focused port that aims to preserve the original DOS behaviour.
nodes.hook: Use for preservation: sometimes the design goal is not enhancement, it is historical accuracy.

nodes.name: PrBoom+ / DSDA-Doom
nodes.note: Speedrunning and demo-compatible branch of Doom port development.
nodes.hook: Shows how competitive play can shape tool and engine priorities.

nodes.name: GZDoom
nodes.note: Feature-rich Doom-family port with advanced rendering and scripting.
nodes.hook: Great for showing how a retro engine can become a modern creation platform.

nodes.name: Zandronum
nodes.note: Multiplayer-focused Doom port lineage from Skulltag.
nodes.hook: Good case study for networking and community server ecosystems.

nodes.name: Brutal Doom
nodes.note: Famous gameplay mod often used through advanced Doom ports.
nodes.hook: Useful to discuss remix culture, controversy, feedback loops and audiovisual game feel.

nodes.name: Quake engine
nodes.note: True 3D polygonal FPS engine. Its source release and licensing influence reached far beyond Quake itself.
nodes.hook: The cleanest classroom jump from 2.5D to true 3D: movement, lighting, BSP, networking and modding all change.

nodes.name: Quake
nodes.note: The showcase game for the original Quake engine.
nodes.hook: Teach movement tech, deathmatch, client/server multiplayer and modding culture.

nodes.name: QuakeWorld
nodes.note: Networking update that made internet play more practical for Quake.
nodes.hook: Excellent for prediction, latency and why netcode is game design.

nodes.name: Team Fortress mod
nodes.note: Class-based Quake mod that became a long-running design lineage.
nodes.hook: Useful example of a mod becoming a commercial design family.

nodes.name: DarkPlaces
nodes.note: Enhanced Quake engine/source port used for standalone projects and visual upgrades.
nodes.hook: Shows how a port can become a platform in its own right.

nodes.name: QuakeSpasm
nodes.note: Popular modern Quake source port for playing and testing classic-style content.
nodes.hook: Use for preservation plus classroom mod testing.

nodes.name: FTEQW
nodes.note: Multi-engine Quake-family source port with broad protocol and format support.
nodes.hook: Good example of compatibility as an engineering challenge.

nodes.name: GoldSrc
nodes.note: Valve's Half-Life engine lineage, based on heavily modified Quake technology rather than being a simple Quake game.
nodes.hook: Branch-root example: teach students why a successor deserves its own branch when it gains its own tools, ecosystem and design identity.

nodes.name: Half-Life
nodes.note: Landmark scripted FPS campaign powered by GoldSrc.
nodes.hook: Teach environmental storytelling, pacing and scripted sequences.

nodes.name: Counter-Strike
nodes.note: Started as a Half-Life mod and became a major tactical FPS series.
nodes.hook: Superb example of mod-to-product transition and asymmetric round design.

nodes.name: Team Fortress Classic
nodes.note: Valve's GoldSrc continuation of class-based Team Fortress design.
nodes.hook: Compare with Quake Team Fortress and Team Fortress 2.

nodes.name: Day of Defeat
nodes.note: GoldSrc WWII mod-to-retail example.
nodes.hook: Useful for discussing historical theme, map control and community development.

nodes.name: Sven Co-op
nodes.note: Co-operative Half-Life mod that became a standalone release.
nodes.hook: Good case for co-op level design and long-lived community maintenance.

nodes.name: Xash3D FWGS
nodes.note: Open-source reimplementation/engine project compatible with GoldSrc content.
nodes.hook: Useful for legal and technical distinctions: compatible reimplementation is not the same as leaked source code.

nodes.name: Quake II engine / id Tech 2
nodes.note: Second-generation Quake-family engine, often labelled id Tech 2 after the fact.
nodes.hook: Compare coloured lighting, DLL game logic and client/server architecture with Quake 1.

nodes.name: Quake II
nodes.note: Showcase title for id Tech 2.
nodes.hook: Use for mission structure and tech evolution from Quake.

nodes.name: SiN
nodes.note: Licensed Quake II engine title with interactive environments.
nodes.hook: Good example of licensed engines becoming differentiated games.

nodes.name: Heretic II
nodes.note: Third-person action game built on Quake II technology.
nodes.hook: Engine lineage does not lock camera perspective.

nodes.name: Kingpin
nodes.note: Quake II-derived shooter notable for dialogue systems and gritty setting.
nodes.hook: Use for tone, content boundaries and systemic NPC interaction.

nodes.name: Daikatana
nodes.note: Heavily modified Quake II engine project; useful as a production cautionary tale.
nodes.hook: Teach scope control and engine modification risk.

nodes.name: Yamagi Quake II
nodes.note: Maintained Quake II source port focused on stability and preservation.
nodes.hook: Good classroom-friendly way to inspect classic engine behaviour.

nodes.name: id Tech 3 / Quake III Arena engine
nodes.note: Arena-focused engine with shaders, VM game code and strong licensing influence.
nodes.hook: Use to discuss rendering pipelines, data-driven materials and multiplayer-first architecture.

nodes.name: Quake III Arena
nodes.note: Arena shooter showcase for id Tech 3.
nodes.hook: Strong design case for pure mechanics, movement skill and map control.

nodes.name: Return to Castle Wolfenstein
nodes.note: id Tech 3 licensed/team FPS lineage.
nodes.hook: Useful bridge from arena combat to class/team objectives.

nodes.name: Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory
nodes.note: Free team/objective FPS based on the RTCW/id Tech 3 lineage.
nodes.hook: Excellent for objective design, class roles and public-server communities.

nodes.name: Jedi Outcast
nodes.note: Raven's id Tech 3-powered Star Wars action game.
nodes.hook: Show how melee systems can be layered onto an FPS engine.

nodes.name: Jedi Academy
nodes.note: Follow-up using the same broad tech lineage with deeper saber customisation.
nodes.hook: Good for avatar identity and progression discussion.

nodes.name: Medal of Honor: Allied Assault
nodes.note: World War II shooter from the id Tech 3 licensing era.
nodes.hook: Useful for cinematic scripting and historical shooter design.

nodes.name: Star Trek: Elite Force
nodes.note: Licensed id Tech 3-era FPS by Raven.
nodes.hook: Good example of adapting an engine to a strong IP identity.

nodes.name: ioquake3
nodes.note: Community-maintained id Tech 3 source-port base used by projects and ports.
nodes.hook: Use to explain open-source maintenance and portability.

nodes.name: OpenArena
nodes.note: Free/open arena shooter using the ioquake3/id Tech 3 ecosystem.
nodes.hook: Good for free-content vs free-code licensing discussion.

nodes.name: Tremulous
nodes.note: Standalone asymmetric shooter/RTS hybrid from the Quake 3 ecosystem.
nodes.hook: Useful for hybrid genre and asymmetry lessons.

nodes.name: Urban Terror
nodes.note: Tactical shooter that grew from Quake III mod roots.
nodes.hook: Compare its tactical movement to Counter-Strike's round structure.

nodes.name: Call of Duty
nodes.note: Early Call of Duty title from the id Tech 3 era.
nodes.hook: Use for cinematic scripting and squad-feel design.

nodes.name: id Tech 4 / Doom 3 engine
nodes.note: Dynamic lighting and stencil-shadow-focused engine, later released through Doom 3 BFG source.
nodes.hook: Use for renderer trade-offs: beautiful shadows versus content/performance constraints.

nodes.name: Doom 3
nodes.note: Horror-focused id Tech 4 showcase.
nodes.hook: Compare how lighting tech directly drives genre tone.

nodes.name: Quake 4
nodes.note: Raven-developed Quake sequel on id Tech 4.
nodes.hook: Good for discussing franchise identity across engine generations.

nodes.name: Prey
nodes.note: id Tech 4 title with portals, gravity shifts and spatial tricks.
nodes.hook: Useful for spatial mechanics and affordance lessons.

nodes.name: Enemy Territory: Quake Wars
nodes.note: Team/objective shooter built from id Tech 4 technology.
nodes.hook: Compare class/objective design with Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory.

nodes.name: The Dark Mod
nodes.note: Stealth-focused standalone project evolved from Doom 3 mod roots.
nodes.hook: Excellent example of engine re-use far outside the original game fantasy.

nodes.name: RBDOOM-3-BFG
nodes.note: Modernised Doom 3 BFG source-port/rendering branch.
nodes.hook: Use to discuss renderer modernisation and legacy code.

nodes.name: id Tech 5
nodes.note: MegaTexture/virtual texturing era, associated with Rage and MachineGames-era titles.
nodes.hook: Use for texture streaming and content pipeline trade-offs.

nodes.name: RAGE
nodes.note: Primary id Tech 5 showcase.
nodes.hook: Good for open-world texture streaming and art pipeline discussion.

nodes.name: Wolfenstein: The New Order
nodes.note: MachineGames title using id Tech 5.
nodes.hook: Discuss narrative shooter pacing within engine constraints.

nodes.name: The Evil Within
nodes.note: Survival horror title built on a modified id Tech 5 lineage.
nodes.hook: Good genre adaptation case.

nodes.name: id Tech 6
nodes.note: Modern id renderer era associated with DOOM (2016).
nodes.hook: Use to discuss 60 FPS combat readability, animation and encounter flow.

nodes.name: DOOM (2016)
nodes.note: Reboot-era Doom combat showcase.
nodes.hook: Teach push-forward combat, glory kills and resource loops.

nodes.name: Wolfenstein II
nodes.note: MachineGames title using id Tech 6-era technology.
nodes.hook: Compare cinematic narrative with high-speed shooter foundations.

nodes.name: id Tech 7
nodes.note: Modern id Tech branch associated with Doom Eternal.
nodes.hook: Good for teaching animation readability, weak-point design and scalable rendering.

nodes.name: DOOM Eternal
nodes.note: id Tech 7 showcase with highly structured combat chess design.
nodes.hook: Excellent for teaching systems design: every enemy, ammo type and movement option has a job.

nodes.name: id Tech 8
nodes.note: Newer id Tech branch used for DOOM: The Dark Ages. Included because it is now a proper successor branch rather than just a game leaf.
nodes.hook: Use as current-generation example: engine iteration supports different combat verbs and scale.

nodes.name: DOOM: The Dark Ages
nodes.note: Modern DOOM prequel powered by id Tech 8.
nodes.hook: Compare with DOOM Eternal: grounded shield/parry rhythm versus aerial resource juggling.

nodes.name: Source
nodes.note: Valve's major engine branch after GoldSrc, strongly associated with Half-Life 2 and Steam-era modding.
nodes.hook: Use to teach physics, facial animation, tools and modding as a platform strategy.

nodes.name: Half-Life 2
nodes.note: Source showcase title with physics-heavy puzzle/action design.
nodes.hook: Gravity Gun = mechanics, engine feature and level design all reinforcing each other.

nodes.name: Counter-Strike: Source
nodes.note: Counter-Strike moved from GoldSrc to Source.
nodes.hook: Compare feel changes when a competitive game moves engine.

nodes.name: Garry's Mod
nodes.note: Sandbox/mod platform built on Source.
nodes.hook: One of the clearest examples of players turning engine affordances into play.

nodes.name: Team Fortress 2
nodes.note: Stylised class shooter in the Team Fortress lineage.
nodes.hook: Compare silhouette, class readability and long-term live balancing.

nodes.name: Portal
nodes.note: Puzzle game built from Source technology and a student-project lineage.
nodes.hook: Great for teaching how one mechanic can carry an entire design.

nodes.name: Left 4 Dead
nodes.note: Co-op zombie shooter with AI Director concept.
nodes.hook: Use for procedural pacing and co-op role pressure.

nodes.name: Respawn modified Source branch
nodes.note: A heavily modified Source-derived commercial branch associated with Titanfall and Apex Legends.
nodes.hook: Good example of when a branch has diverged enough to deserve its own node.

nodes.name: Titanfall
nodes.note: Fast movement/mech shooter from the modified Source branch.
nodes.hook: Teach traversal verbs and readability at speed.

nodes.name: Apex Legends
nodes.note: Battle royale/hero shooter from Respawn's modified Source branch.
nodes.hook: Excellent for class-based battle royale design and ping communication systems.

nodes.name: Source 2
nodes.note: Valve's successor to Source. Used in modern Valve titles and tools.
nodes.hook: Compare upgrade/migration problems when live games move engine generations.

nodes.name: Dota 2
nodes.note: Valve MOBA that moved from Source to Source 2 through the Reborn update; a major long-running esport.
nodes.hook: Use for MOBAs, live-service migration, spectator UX and esports production stability.

nodes.name: Half-Life: Alyx
nodes.note: VR showcase title for Source 2.
nodes.hook: Use to teach embodiment, hand interaction and VR environmental design.

nodes.name: Counter-Strike 2
nodes.note: Counter-Strike's Source 2 migration.
nodes.hook: Great for technical debate: visual clarity, subtick/netcode claims, smoke systems and competitive acceptance.

nodes.name: Unreal lineage
nodes.note: Epic's long-running general-purpose commercial engine lineage.
nodes.hook: Counterpoint to id: Unreal becomes a broad production platform, not just a shooter engine family.

nodes.name: Unreal Engine 1
nodes.note: Original Unreal/Unreal Tournament-era engine.
nodes.hook: Compare software rendering, early hardware acceleration and mod tools with Quake-era engines.

nodes.name: Unreal
nodes.note: Original showcase for Unreal Engine.
nodes.hook: Use for environmental spectacle and technology-led world presentation.

nodes.name: Unreal Tournament
nodes.note: Arena shooter that competed with Quake III.
nodes.hook: Directly compare arena design with Quake III Arena.

nodes.name: Deus Ex
nodes.note: Immersive sim built on Unreal technology.
nodes.hook: Strong example of an FPS engine supporting RPG/systems design.

nodes.name: Unreal Engine 2
nodes.note: Second major Unreal generation with broad licensing use.
nodes.hook: Use to discuss middleware becoming a business model.

nodes.name: Unreal Tournament 2004
nodes.note: Arena/vehicle combat showcase.
nodes.hook: Compare movement, vehicles and map scale.

nodes.name: Splinter Cell
nodes.note: Stealth franchise associated with Unreal Engine 2-era tech.
nodes.hook: Discuss lighting, stealth readability and engine adaptation.

nodes.name: BioShock
nodes.note: Heavily modified Unreal Engine 2.5-era immersive shooter.
nodes.hook: Good for worldbuilding and systemic ability design.

nodes.name: Unreal Engine 3
nodes.note: Very widely licensed HD-console-era Unreal generation.
nodes.hook: Use for pipeline standardisation, normal maps, middleware and console-era production.

nodes.name: Gears of War
nodes.note: UE3 showcase for cover shooting and HD visuals.
nodes.hook: Teach camera, cover and readability in third-person combat.

nodes.name: Mass Effect
nodes.note: RPG/shooter franchise built on UE3.
nodes.hook: Useful for dialogue, squad systems and cinematic RPG production.

nodes.name: Batman: Arkham Asylum
nodes.note: UE3 action-adventure benchmark.
nodes.hook: Teach combat rhythm, predator stealth and adaptation of IP into mechanics.

nodes.name: Borderlands
nodes.note: UE3 looter-shooter with strong stylisation.
nodes.hook: Use for art direction overriding assumptions about engine look.

nodes.name: Unreal Engine 4
nodes.note: UE4 expanded Blueprint workflows and broader indie/education access.
nodes.hook: Useful for teaching visual scripting, prototyping and accessible production pipelines.

nodes.name: Fortnite
nodes.note: UE4 live-service battle royale and platform ecosystem.
nodes.hook: Use for live ops, crossovers, creative mode and UGC as retention.

nodes.name: PUBG
nodes.note: Battle royale title built with UE4.
nodes.hook: Compare with Fortnite and Apex: same broad genre, different movement/readability/design priorities.

nodes.name: Final Fantasy VII Remake
nodes.note: Large-scale RPG production using UE4.
nodes.hook: Shows Unreal's range outside shooters.

nodes.name: VALORANT
nodes.note: Competitive tactical shooter built on UE4.
nodes.hook: Great for esports lessons: tick rate, anti-cheat, silhouettes and ability clarity.

nodes.name: Unreal Engine 5
nodes.note: Current Unreal generation associated with Nanite, Lumen, World Partition and modern virtual production workflows.
nodes.hook: Use for teaching asset scale, lighting iteration and modern production expectations.

nodes.name: Fortnite UE5 transition
nodes.note: Fortnite moved into UE5-era technology.
nodes.hook: Useful live-service migration example.

nodes.name: Hellblade II
nodes.note: High-fidelity UE5 cinematic action title.
nodes.hook: Discuss capture, cinematics and visual fidelity trade-offs.

nodes.name: S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2
nodes.note: Large UE5 open-world shooter example.
nodes.hook: Use for streaming, atmosphere, AI, open-world performance.

nodes.name: Build engine lineage
nodes.note: Ken Silverman's Build engine and its games/source-port descendants.
nodes.hook: Counterpoint to Doom: both are 2.5D-ish but have different mapping affordances and editor cultures.

nodes.name: Build Engine
nodes.note: Sector/sprite FPS engine best known through Duke Nukem 3D, Shadow Warrior and Blood.
nodes.hook: Teach vertical illusion, sectors, interactivity, room-over-room tricks and why level editors shape design.

nodes.name: Witchaven
nodes.note: Early licensed Build Engine game.
nodes.hook: Useful for comparing first use versus most famous use.

nodes.name: Duke Nukem 3D
nodes.note: Most famous Build Engine showcase.
nodes.hook: Use for environmental interactivity and real-world spaces in level design.

nodes.name: Shadow Warrior
nodes.note: Build Engine shooter with vehicles and advanced interactivity for its era.
nodes.hook: Discuss iteration on tools and level trickery.

nodes.name: Blood
nodes.note: Cult Build Engine horror shooter.
nodes.hook: Strong case for mood, weapon feel and enemy personality inside constrained tech.

nodes.name: EDuke32
nodes.note: Modern Build/Duke3D source-port ecosystem used for preservation and new projects.
nodes.hook: Use for how source ports extend old engines into new production environments.

nodes.name: Ion Fury
nodes.note: Modern commercial game built with EDuke32/Build technology.
nodes.hook: Excellent for retro-modern design: old constraints plus modern expectations.

nodes.name: Selaco
nodes.note: Modern commercial GZDoom-based shooter.
nodes.hook: Great for showing that source-port ecosystems can support modern-feeling games.

nodes.name: Build 2
nodes.note: Ken Silverman's experimental successor to Build, later released publicly as demos/tools.
nodes.hook: Useful successor discussion: not every technical successor becomes a mainstream production lineage.

nodes.name: Crytek / CryEngine lineage
nodes.note: CryEngine lineage with major forks to Ubisoft Dunia and Amazon Lumberyard, then O3DE.
nodes.hook: Great for teaching commercial engine branching and downstream open-source transitions.

nodes.name: CryEngine 1
nodes.note: First generation CryEngine used in early Far Cry era.
nodes.hook: Use for early 2000s rendering leaps and vegetation-heavy worlds.

nodes.name: Far Cry
nodes.note: Flagship early title for CryEngine 1.
nodes.hook: Demonstrates open environments and AI encounter pacing.

nodes.name: CryEngine 2
nodes.note: Crysis-era successor engine.
nodes.hook: Great for discussing hardware stress tests and visual targets.

nodes.name: Crysis
nodes.note: Landmark visual showcase for CryEngine 2.
nodes.hook: Useful for optimization discussions and scalability.

nodes.name: CryEngine 3
nodes.note: Major rewrite targeting wider platforms and console workflows.
nodes.hook: Shows portability and iteration in AAA engines.

nodes.name: CryEngine V
nodes.note: Modern CryEngine branding/version era.
nodes.hook: Use to discuss business model shifts and engine longevity.

nodes.name: Dunia Engine
nodes.note: Ubisoft fork rooted in early CryEngine technology.
nodes.hook: Case study: internal forks become long-term proprietary platforms.

nodes.name: Far Cry 3
nodes.note: High-profile Dunia title.
nodes.hook: Useful for open-world systems design examples.

nodes.name: Amazon Lumberyard
nodes.note: Amazon's CryEngine-derived platform.
nodes.hook: Shows cloud/platform strategy influencing engine architecture.

nodes.name: Open 3D Engine (O3DE)
nodes.note: Open-source successor derived from Lumberyard foundations.
nodes.hook: Good example of proprietary-to-open governance shift.

nodes.name: Bethesda RPG tech lineage
nodes.note: NetImmerse and Gamebryo descendants through Creation Engine generations.
nodes.hook: Excellent lineage for discussing long-lived world-simulation tooling.

nodes.name: NetImmerse
nodes.note: Predecessor technology that evolved into Gamebryo.
nodes.hook: Teaches rebranding and engine evolution over decades.

nodes.name: Gamebryo
nodes.note: Commercial engine lineage used by many studios and RPGs.
nodes.hook: Great for middleware-era licensing discussions.

nodes.name: The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind
nodes.note: Bethesda RPG era linked to NetImmerse roots.
nodes.hook: Useful for systemic RPG design and modding history.

nodes.name: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion
nodes.note: Major Gamebryo-era Bethesda release.
nodes.hook: Shows world streaming and quest-scripting evolution.

nodes.name: Creation Engine
nodes.note: Bethesda's internal evolution from Gamebryo technology.
nodes.hook: Discusses engine continuity vs architectural rewrites.

nodes.name: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim
nodes.note: Flagship Creation Engine title.
nodes.hook: Useful for systems-heavy open-world comparisons.

nodes.name: Creation Engine 2
nodes.note: Second major Creation generation used in Starfield.
nodes.hook: Use to discuss generational upgrades in long-lived engines.

nodes.name: Starfield
nodes.note: Early high-profile Creation Engine 2 game.
nodes.hook: Useful for discussing simulation complexity and scale.

nodes.name: EA DICE Frostbite lineage
nodes.note: Frostbite generations used across EA first-party studios.
nodes.hook: Good case for centralized studio engine strategy.

nodes.name: Frostbite 1
nodes.note: First Frostbite generation for Battlefield: Bad Company.
nodes.hook: Highlights destruction-focused rendering and physics priorities.

nodes.name: Battlefield: Bad Company
nodes.note: Launch-era Frostbite title.
nodes.hook: Useful for discussing destructible level design.

nodes.name: Frostbite 2
nodes.note: Second-generation Frostbite with broader production capabilities.
nodes.hook: Discusses scale-up from single-franchise to multi-studio use.

nodes.name: Frostbite 3
nodes.note: Cross-genre Frostbite generation used by many EA teams.
nodes.hook: Great for talking about internal platform standardization.

nodes.name: Rockstar engine lineage
nodes.note: From RenderWare-era games to Rockstar's RAGE platform.
nodes.hook: Good for teaching middleware-to-internal transitions.

nodes.name: RenderWare
nodes.note: Widely licensed middleware used in many PS2-era games.
nodes.hook: Use for middleware history and cross-studio tooling.

nodes.name: GTA: San Andreas
nodes.note: Major RenderWare-era Rockstar title.
nodes.hook: Useful for open-world mission system analysis.

nodes.name: Rockstar Advanced Game Engine (RAGE)
nodes.note: Rockstar Advanced Game Engine succeeding RenderWare usage.
nodes.hook: Shows pivot from licensed middleware to internal platform control.

nodes.name: Grand Theft Auto V
nodes.note: Landmark RAGE release.
nodes.hook: Use for world streaming and mission scripting at scale.

nodes.name: Red Dead Redemption 2
nodes.note: Advanced RAGE-era simulation title.
nodes.hook: Great example for systemic AI and simulation fidelity trade-offs.

nodes.name: Ubisoft proprietary lineage
nodes.note: Ubisoft's internal engine branches including Dunia, Anvil and Snowdrop.
nodes.hook: Useful to compare parallel in-house engine strategies inside one publisher.

nodes.name: Anvil (Scimitar)
nodes.note: Assassin's Creed engine line origin.
nodes.hook: Good for crowds, traversal and animation pipeline discussions.

nodes.name: AnvilNext / AnvilNext 2.0
nodes.note: Successive Anvil generation upgrades for AC series scale.
nodes.hook: Shows iterative improvements under annualized production pressure.

nodes.name: Snowdrop
nodes.note: Massive Entertainment engine used across several Ubisoft projects.
nodes.hook: Great case for studio-built tech spreading publisher-wide.

nodes.name: Capcom engine lineage
nodes.note: From MT Framework toward RE Engine.
nodes.hook: Useful for discussing transitions between console generations.

nodes.name: MT Framework
nodes.note: Capcom's long-running internal engine for many major titles.
nodes.hook: Good for cross-franchise reuse and platform adaptation.

nodes.name: Panta Rhei
nodes.note: Experimental successor path associated with Deep Down era.
nodes.hook: Teaches that not every branch becomes the dominant production line.

nodes.name: RE Engine
nodes.note: Modern Capcom engine used widely across Resident Evil and other franchises.
nodes.hook: Useful for discussing modern lighting/material workflows.

nodes.name: Resident Evil 2 (Remake)
nodes.note: Major RE Engine showcase release.
nodes.hook: Excellent for atmospheric rendering and encounter pacing analysis.

nodes.name: Unity lineage
nodes.note: Unity major generation milestones and ecosystem growth.
nodes.hook: Good for cross-platform engine economics and tooling discussions.

nodes.name: Unity (initial release)
nodes.note: Early Unity release era.
nodes.hook: Highlights democratization of game production tooling.

nodes.name: Unity 5
nodes.note: Major generation with physically based rendering era upgrades.
nodes.hook: Use for PBR pipeline discussion in accessible engines.

nodes.name: Unity 2021+ LTS era
nodes.note: Modern long-term-support branch used in production pipelines.
nodes.hook: Useful for stability vs feature cadence debates.

nodes.name: Pokémon GO
nodes.note: High-profile Unity title at global scale.
nodes.hook: Good for mobile/live-service engineering discussions.

nodes.name: Godot lineage
nodes.note: Open-source Godot generational path.
nodes.hook: Good case study for community-led engine evolution.

nodes.name: Godot 1.x
nodes.note: Initial open-source public era.
nodes.hook: Use for open governance and contributor ecosystem discussions.

nodes.name: Godot 2.x
nodes.note: Second major generation with broader usability.
nodes.hook: Shows iterative UX/tooling improvements in OSS engines.

nodes.name: Godot 3.x
nodes.note: Matured 3.x line with wide adoption.
nodes.hook: Good for discussing adoption tipping points.

nodes.name: Godot 4.x
nodes.note: Current major generation with renderer and workflow changes.
nodes.hook: Useful for migration planning and compatibility discussions.

nodes.name: AnvilNext 2.0
nodes.note: Ground-up rebuild phase for dense city simulation and updated rendering.
nodes.hook: Good case for major internal rewrites between generation cycles.

nodes.name: Ubisoft Anvil
nodes.note: Rebranded modern Anvil generation beginning with Valhalla era.
